lead: Every liquid–liquid contactor does two jobs: it disperses one liquid as drops in the other to make interfacial area for mass transfer, and it then lets the drops coalesce so the layers can be separated. Stage-wise equipment (mixer-settlers) does the two jobs in separate vessels, one stage per unit. Differential contactors (spray, packed and mechanically agitated columns) do both continuously in one tall vessel with the liquids in counter-current flow, and are sized by transfer units rather than stages. The choice depends on the number of stages, throughput, floor space, settling behaviour and how much solvent the plant can afford to hold.
prereq: You need Multistage counter-current extraction (extraction factor, ideal stages).

blocks.text: A mixer-settler stage is a stirred tank followed by a settling tank. The mixer is sized by residence time t = V/Q (V mixer volume, Q total flow of both liquids); a few minutes usually brings the stage close to equilibrium, giving stage efficiencies of about 0.8 to 1. The settler is a horizontal tank in which the drops must rise or fall across the layer while the liquid flows to the far end. Like a clarifier, its plan area must be large enough that the upward or downward speed of the continuous liquid is smaller than the settling velocity of the drops: A ≥ Q<sub>c</sub>/u<sub>t</sub>.

blocks.where: Stokes settling velocity of a small drop (Reynolds number below about 1): Δρ is the density difference (kg/m³), d the drop diameter (m), μ<sub>c</sub> the viscosity of the continuous liquid (Pa·s), g = 9.81 m/s².

blocks.text: Mixer-settlers give reliable, easily scaled stages, tolerate solids and high flows, and a battery can be extended stage by stage. Their costs are floor space, a large inventory of (often flammable) solvent, and pumping or gravity flow between stages.

sections.h3: Column contactors: spray, packed and agitated

items: Spray column: an empty shell with a distributor that sprays the dispersed liquid as drops through the continuous liquid. Cheap and hard to foul, but the continuous phase back-mixes badly, so one spray column rarely gives more than one or two stages.

Packed column: random or structured packing breaks and re-forms the drops and limits back-mixing, giving several stages. The packing should be wetted by the continuous phase, so the dispersed liquid stays as drops instead of a film. Capacity is limited by flooding.
Sieve-tray column: the dispersed liquid coalesces under (or over) each perforated tray and is re-dispersed through the holes, so each tray acts roughly as a stage.

Mechanically agitated columns: the rotating-disc contactor (RDC) has discs on a central shaft between stator rings; the Scheibel and Oldshue–Rushton columns have impellers between calming zones; the Karr column moves a stack of perforated plates up and down. Agitation makes smaller drops and more area, so the height per stage is much less.

blocks.text: Flooding is the condition where the dispersed drops can no longer pass through the continuous phase and one liquid is carried out with the other. Columns are designed at about 50 to 70 % of the flooding throughput, which fixes the cross-sectional area: A = (Qc + Qd)/(allowable total superficial velocity).
Z = H<sub>OR</sub> N<sub>OR</sub>;   N<sub>OR</sub> = ln[ ((x<sub>1</sub> − y<sub>2</sub>/m)/(x<sub>2</sub> − y<sub>2</sub>/m))(1 − 1/ε) + 1/ε ] / (1 − 1/ε)
blocks.where: Height of a column contactor for dilute solutions with a straight equilibrium line y = mx. x<sub>1</sub> and x<sub>2</sub> are the solute concentrations of the raffinate phase entering and leaving; y<sub>2</sub> is that of the entering solvent; ε = mS/R is the extraction factor on the flow basis used for m; H<sub>OR</sub> is the overall height of a transfer unit based on the raffinate phase (m), from pilot data or correlations.

sections.h3: Packed extraction with reflux, and choosing a contactor

blocks.text: With a simple counter-current column the extract can be no richer than equilibrium with the feed. When the solvent is selective but dissolves some carrier, part of the solvent-free extract product is returned to the extract end of the column as extract reflux. Above the feed point the reflux strips carrier out of the extract, as the rectifying section of a distillation column enriches the vapour. The feed then enters part way up, the column has an enriching and a stripping section, and the extract product can be much purer than with plain counter-current flow.

examples.question: A mixer-settler handles 12 m³/h of combined liquids in a 0.5 m³ mixer. In the settler the continuous phase flows at 8 m³/h, the drops are 150 µm, Δρ = 150 kg/m³ and μ<sub>c</sub> = 1.0 mPa·s. Find the mixer residence time and the minimum settler area.
steps: Residence time t = V/Q = 0.5/12 = 0.0417 h = 2.5 min.
Check Stokes' law: Re = ρ u<sub>t</sub> d/μ = 1000 × 1.84 × 10⁻³ × 150 × 10⁻⁶/10⁻³ = 0.28, below 1, so the law holds.
Settler area A = Q<sub>c</sub>/u<sub>t</sub> = 8/6.62 = 1.21 m²; a practical settler adds a margin for the dispersion band.
examples.answer: The mixer gives 2.5 min of contact; the settler needs at least 1.21 m² of plan area.

examples.question: A packed column must remove 90 % of a solute from a dilute aqueous feed (x<sub>1</sub> = 0.04 to x<sub>2</sub> = 0.004 kg/kg) with pure solvent at ε = mS/R = 1.5. Pilot tests give H<sub>OR</sub> = 0.9 m. The flows are 20 m³/h continuous and 15 m³/h dispersed, and the allowable total superficial velocity is 21 m/h (60 % of flooding). Find the height and diameter.
steps: With y<sub>2</sub> = 0: ratio x<sub>1</sub>/x<sub>2</sub> = 10, and N<sub>OR</sub> = ln(10 × 0.3333 + 0.6667)/0.3333 = ln 4.0/0.3333 = 1.386/0.3333 = 4.16 transfer units.
Height Z = 0.9 × 4.16 = 3.74 m of packing (add distributor and settling zones at each end).
examples.answer: About 4.16 transfer units, 3.74 m of packing in a 1.46 m diameter column.

traps: The settler area depends on the flow of the continuous liquid through which the drops settle, and on the drop settling velocity; the mixer volume sets only the contact time.
Stokes' law needs Re below about 1; check it, and use the continuous-phase viscosity.
The packing must be wetted by the continuous phase; if the dispersed phase wets it, the drops spread into films and the area falls.
A spray column is not many stages: back-mixing of the continuous phase limits it to one or two.
Transfer units (N<sub>OR</sub> = 4.16) are not ideal stages; they become equal only when ε = 1.

quiz.q: What two jobs must every extraction contactor do?
quiz.a: Disperse one liquid in the other to create interfacial area, and then coalesce and separate the two layers.

quiz.q: Name three mechanically agitated extraction columns.
quiz.a: Rotating-disc contactor (RDC), Scheibel column, Karr reciprocating-plate column (also the Oldshue–Rushton column).

quiz.q: Why does a spray column give few stages even when it is tall?
quiz.a: The continuous phase circulates and back-mixes along the column, so its concentration evens out and the counter-current driving force is lost; height adds little separation.

quiz.q: What does extract reflux do in packed-bed extraction?
quiz.a: Solvent-free extract product returned to the extract end washes carrier out of the rising extract, as reflux enriches the vapour in distillation, so the extract product is purer than plain counter-current contact allows.

quiz.q: A mixer of 0.8 m³ takes 4 m³/h of combined flow. Find the residence time.
Find N<sub>OR</sub> for 95 % removal (x<sub>1</sub>/x<sub>2</sub> = 20) with pure solvent and ε = 2.
Choose a contactor for 8 stages of clean, low-viscosity liquids at 50 m³/h with a flammable solvent, and justify it.
quiz.a: A mechanically agitated column (RDC or Karr): 8 stages fit in one shell of modest height, floor space is small and the solvent hold-up is low, which matters for a flammable solvent. A mixer-settler battery would need 8 tanks and settlers and hold much more solvent; a spray or plain packed column could not give 8 stages.

beyond: Not for the exam. Column design today uses drop population balances with CFD to predict hold-up and drop size, checked by small pilot columns of the chosen type. Membrane contactors keep the two liquids on either side of a porous hollow fibre, so they never flood or emulsify. Miniature mixer-settlers and centrifugal contactors are used for continuous pharmaceutical production. Search for RDC column design, axial dispersion in extraction columns and hollow-fibre membrane contactor.
